summary: Money and dates, exactly, on the one maths core. Two new line forms that need no problem sheet, `math money | ...` and `math dates | ...`, take the same four verbs as the sheet's line (calculate, solve, range, check), with amounts (1200 USD) and dates (2026-11-20, 30 days, 1 month) written inside the expression. Dates also get two calendar verbs: `deadline N UNIT after DATE [| end included|excluded]` and `business days FROM TO`, both with an optional `| holidays D ...`. They compile to two new read operations, math.money and math.dates. A new frame, workbench/math_typed.py, checks the kind of every value first: the currency, or date / number of days / plain number. A mix nobody asked for (USD + EUR, a date plus a date, a date plus a bare number) is refused in words. The expression then goes unchanged, as plain exact Fractions, through math_answers.ask over math_ranges: the same states, guarantee and steps. The ledger.math-answer/1 record that comes back is relabelled in the kinds: every number carries its currency code, 'date' with its ISO date beside it, or 'days'. A `money` or `calendar` field records the currencies, rates, conversions and rounding, or the calendar steps, clamping, holidays and their source. The words and receipt are the frame's own: amounts with currency and exact value, dates with their weekday, never a code or an operation name. No frozen file is touched. Six worked examples are on the lines page (docs/INTEGRATED_I02.md) and run word for word in a test. Kasandra's tool selection gets a money-and-dates family, so she is offered these lines for a budget or a deadline and not for plotting a voltage. A line she proposes never carries a range, an exchange rate or a holiday list.

decisions: Where it fits. A currency or a date cannot be a unit of math_units without changing that frozen file: its dimensions are four fixed bases. So the kinds are checked in a new frame (math_typed.py), and the expression then goes to the unchanged core as plain exact fractions. The answer comes back relabelled in the kinds and sealed with the frame's words. No frozen file is touched; math_answers, math_ranges and math_model are only called.

The grammar is the simplest for the owner: no sheet (his own numbers are in the line), the same four verbs he already has, amounts and dates written inside the expression. Only the two rules that are not arithmetic get verbs of their own: deadline and business days. `given NAME A [B] [CODE|days|weeks]` takes a single value or a range. Up to 8 givens per line; at most 4 ranged, the core's own bound.

Rounding rule: half away from zero, and only that one. Bills, bank statements and the euro conversion rules round this way, so a rounded figure matches the owner's papers. Half to even is unbiased over many sums but would differ from them by a cent at every even half. Rounding is offered only as `| round STEP` in calculate and range, and the exact value is always kept beside the result. In solve, `| step 0.01` rounds an allowance inward (never up), as the core does.

On screen an amount shows at least its currency's minor-unit places: 2 by default, 0 for JPY and the like, 3 for KWD and the like. An amount that does not end within its cents is shown to the cent, outward for a range and inward for an allowed end, with the exact fraction beside it. That follows the core's display convention; it is not rounding of the value.

An exchange rate is accepted only from the line (`| rate EUR USD 1.08`: 1 EUR = 1.08 USD), as a positive exact decimal. At most four, and none into a currency that is itself converted. Amounts are converted before any work, and the receipt names the rate and each conversion. An amount times an amount is refused; an amount over an amount of the same currency is a plain number.

The kind of the name being solved for is inferred: the first candidate under which the line's kinds fit (money: plain number, then each currency in the line; dates: date, days, plain number). So `solve "4 * weekly <= 1200 USD" for weekly` answers in USD with nothing more said.

Dates are proleptic Gregorian day numbers (Python's ordinal); dates and day counts are whole (integer domain), so solve gives whole days without a step. Months and years are counted only on a written date, or a name given one date, just before them, left to right, and clamped to the month's last day. Years are 12 months, so 29 Feb + 1 year = 28 Feb. Anything else with months, years or business days is refused in words, because calendar months are not linear.

Deadline rule, stated in the answer, the lines and the receipt: the date is day 0 and counting starts the next day; the end is the date plus N. 'end included' makes the last day inside the period the end day; 'end excluded' makes it the day before. If the line says neither, both are shown and the owner is asked to say which, so no convention is hidden. Only 'after' is a verb; a date before is `calculate "DATE - N days"`.

Business days are Monday to Friday. A count runs from the day after FROM up to and including TO (said on screen). Holidays come only from a list typed in the line (`| holidays D ...`, up to 30) and are named in the receipt; with none, the receipt says no holidays were counted. The plan said 'a list the owner admits as a source'; this build takes the line itself as that admission.

The owner's own: a range, an exchange rate and a holiday list are refused in a line Kasandra proposes, extending the core's 'ranges are the owner's' rule through stac_bridge.owners_only. A single amount or date is part of the question and may be proposed.

Tool selection: math.money and math.dates form their own family, read before the calculator's 'math.' prefix (FIRST_FAMILIES in tool_selection.py). Without it, math.dates was offered for a voltage plot and broke the plan profile's size bound in test_tool_selection.

Each record keeps schema ledger.math-answer/1, with one added field, `money` or `calendar`. Its numbers carry their unit as the currency code, 'date' (plus 'iso') or 'days'. The derivation is retold in the kinds, since the core's steps would show day numbers or four figures. The freshness is CURRENT, because the line has no sheet, and the receipt says every number came from the line. The implementation hashes cover the core and the three new files.
Test module name: test_math_money_dates, listed in tools/check_hatch.py FOCUSED_MODULES on its own line with its own comment, after 'test_math_core','test_math_lines'.

release_note: You can now ask Graphite about money and dates in a line, with your own numbers and no sheet needed. For example: what you can spend each week and stay under the month's budget, which of two loans costs more in total, when a 30-day notice period actually ends, or the date 10 business days from an invoice. Amounts keep their currency and are exact to the last digit. Two currencies are never mixed unless you give the rate, and nothing is rounded unless you ask; then it rounds half away from zero, as your bank does, with the exact amount beside it. Dates show their weekday, months are counted the calendar's way (31 January plus a month is the last day of February), only holidays you list are skipped, and a deadline says whether its last day counts. It works out what you ask from your numbers and your rules; it gives no financial or legal advice.
